pages.title: Can an atom have smaller pieces?

blocks.text: Rub a plastic comb through dry hair and it can attract tiny paper pieces. Electrical behaviour asks a question that an indivisible, featureless atom cannot answer: what inside matter carries electric charge?
Scientists investigated this through controlled experiments. Our task is to connect each observation to the particle it reveals, rather than memorising discovery names.

pages.title: Follow a beam through a discharge tube

blocks.text: In a discharge tube, a high voltage is applied between electrodes in gas at very low pressure. The negative electrode is the cathode; the positive electrode is the anode. A beam travels from cathode towards anode.

A fluorescent coating glows where the beam strikes. The beam travels in straight lines without fields and can cast a shadow. These observations establish a moving beam, but do not yet identify its charge.

Low pressure reduces collisions between beam particles and gas particles, making their path easier to study. High voltage provides the electric conditions for the discharge. The experimental arrangement is designed to reveal motion, rather than imitate conditions inside an ordinary room.

pages.title: Why cathode rays mean electrons

blocks.text: Cathode rays bend towards a positive plate and away from a negative plate. Opposite charges attract, so their particles carry negative charge. These particles are electrons.
Their properties do not depend on gas or electrode material. This repeated result matters: electrons are constituents of atoms generally, rather than an unusual substance released by one metal.
The shadow establishes approximately straight travel; deflection towards the positive plate establishes negative charge. Different observations answer different questions.

A magnetic field can also deflect the moving beam. Combining the electric and magnetic observations links the beam with moving charged particles. Fluorescence alone would not have established its charge: visible effects must be interpreted alongside the field response.

pages.title: Measure charge relative to mass

blocks.text: Thomson studied electron-beam deflection by electric and magnetic fields. His measurement gave the magnitude of the electron charge-to-mass ratio: e/mₑ = 1.758820 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.
Here e is elementary charge magnitude and mₑ electron mass. A large ratio can mean large charge, small mass, or both. The ratio alone cannot determine the two separately.

Compare ratios before separating quantities. If two objects have the same charge magnitude but one has much smaller mass, that object changes motion more readily in the same electric field. This makes deflection a useful clue to charge relative to mass.

pages.title: Oil drops reveal charge magnitude

blocks.text: Millikan measured charged oil drops moving in an electric field. Their charge magnitudes were whole-number multiples of one small charge: |q| = ne, where n is an integer and e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
This is charge quantisation: isolated ordinary charges occur in integral steps. An electron carries −e. A drop with three extra electrons has q=−3e, not an arbitrary fraction of e.

A measured drop charge magnitude of 4.806 × 10⁻¹⁹ C corresponds to n=|q|/e=(4.806 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹)=3. If the drop is negative, it carries three excess electrons. The sign identifies excess negative charge; the integer gives the count.

pages.title: Calculate an electron mass

blocks.text: Teacher-worked application: given e=1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and e/mₑ=1.758820 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹, find mₑ. Rearrange: mₑ=e÷(e/mₑ).
Substitute: mₑ=(1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.758820 × 10¹¹) kg=(1.602/1.758820) × 10⁻³⁰ kg≈9.108 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Rounded inputs explain the slight difference from tabulated 9.1094 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

In the mass calculation, dividing powers means subtracting exponents: 10⁻¹⁹/10¹¹=10⁻³⁰. Since 1.602/1.758820 is less than 1, rewrite approximately 0.9108 × 10⁻³⁰ as 9.108 × 10⁻³¹. The C units cancel, leaving kg.

pages.title: Positive rays tell a different story

blocks.text: In a modified discharge tube, a perforated cathode lets positive particles pass through its holes. These canal rays bend oppositely to electrons in an electric field. They are positive ions of the gas.
Unlike electron properties, their charge-to-mass ratios depend on the gas. The lightest positive ion comes from hydrogen and is the proton. Not every canal-ray particle is a proton.

Hydrogen gas produces the lightest positive ion because removing its sole electron leaves one proton. A heavier gas produces heavier positive ions. This explains why canal-ray measurements vary with gas while the cathode-ray electron measurements remain the same.

pages.title: Find an electrically neutral particle

blocks.text: In 1932 Chadwick bombarded beryllium with α-particles and identified penetrating electrically neutral particles called neutrons. Their existence helped account for nuclear mass beyond the proton contribution.
A neutron has no charge and slightly greater mass than a proton. An electric field therefore does not deflect it as it deflects a charged particle. Neutral does not mean massless.
A ball can have no net electric charge but still have mass. Neutrality describes electric charge, a different property from mass.

The neutron discovery addresses a different question from Millikan’s work. Millikan measures electric charge; Chadwick identifies a neutral massive particle. Neither result can replace the other, because knowing charge alone cannot account for all atomic mass.

pages.title: Compare charge and mass separately

blocks.text: An electron has charge −e and mass about 9.1094 × 10⁻³¹ kg. A proton has charge +e and mass about 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. A neutron has zero charge and mass about 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
The proton and electron have equal charge magnitudes but very unequal masses: the proton is roughly 1836 times heavier. Equal and opposite charges do not imply equal masses.

pages.title: Reconstruct the discoveries

blocks.text: Cathode-ray deflection identifies negative particles; independence from gas and electrodes establishes their universal presence. Thomson measured e/mₑ, while Millikan separately measured e. Combining them gives electron mass.

Canal rays reveal positive gas ions; hydrogen yields the proton. Chadwick established the neutron. Keep each experiment connected to its actual evidence: charge sign, charge magnitude, mass and universality are distinct conclusions.

questions.question: Why does deflection towards a positive plate identify negative charge?
questions.answer: Opposite charges attract, so the direction of deflection establishes the beam particles’ negative charge.

questions.question: Why repeat cathode-ray experiments with different gases?
questions.answer: The unchanged particle properties show that electrons are common constituents of different atoms.

questions.question: Can e/mₑ alone give electron mass?
questions.answer: No. A separate charge measurement is necessary; then mₑ=e/(e/mₑ).

questions.question: What does q=ne tell us about an oil drop?
questions.answer: Its charge is an integral multiple of elementary charge, rather than any arbitrary value.

questions.question: Are canal rays identical for every gas?
questions.answer: No. They contain gas-derived positive ions with different masses and charge-to-mass ratios.

questions.question: How can a neutron be neutral but massive?
questions.answer: Charge and mass are different properties. Zero charge does not imply zero mass.

pages.title: Organise a growing collection of elements

blocks.text: Imagine learning every element as an unrelated list of facts. A classification system helps us find similarities and predict behaviour, much as arranging books by subject helps locate related ideas.
The periodic table is powerful because it organises chemical evidence. Its historical development shows how scientists tested possible patterns and refined the quantity used for ordering.

A family classification makes an unfamiliar item less unfamiliar: knowing it belongs to a set suggests properties to test. In chemistry, those predictions must be checked experimentally. Family membership suggests behaviour; it does not make all members identical.

pages.title: Recognise Döbereiner’s triads

blocks.text: Döbereiner found groups of three chemically similar elements. In some triads, the middle element’s atomic mass was approximately the average of the other two. Lithium, sodium and potassium supplied a useful example.
Using approximate masses 7, 23, 39: (7+39)/2=23, matching sodium. This arithmetic is a pattern in selected families, not a rule that groups every element into a successful triad.

pages.title: Test Newlands’ octaves

blocks.text: Newlands arranged elements in increasing atomic mass and observed that every eighth resembled the first, analogous to repeating musical notes. His law of octaves worked reasonably for lighter elements up to calcium.
Beyond that region, unlike elements could be forced together and similar ones separated. The failure matters: an appealing pattern must agree with chemistry rather than control it.

pages.title: Understand Mendeleev’s periodic law

blocks.text: Mendeleev related elemental properties periodically to atomic masses. He placed chemically similar elements in groups and used compounds’ formulas as evidence for family membership.
He did not insist on mass order when strong chemical evidence disagreed. Tellurium and iodine illustrate why chemical similarity could be more informative than a strictly increasing mass list.

pages.title: Replace atomic mass with atomic number

blocks.text: Moseley’s work established atomic number, or nuclear proton number Z, as the fundamental ordering quantity. Modern periodic law states that physical and chemical properties are periodic functions of atomic number.
Atomic mass can vary among isotopes without changing the element. Atomic number does not: it fixes the nuclear identity. Increasing Z provides a consistent ordering principle.

pages.title: Explain why properties repeat

blocks.text: As atomic number increases, electron configurations change in an ordered way. Similar valence-shell arrangements recur, so certain chemical properties recur. Periodicity is an electronic pattern, not a magical repetition after a fixed count in every row.
Lithium and sodium each have one electron outside a noble-gas core. That similarity helps explain their family relationship even though their masses and total electron counts differ.

pages.title: Why do atoms stay together?

blocks.text: Hydrogen and oxygen combine into water with properties unlike either element. A chemical bond is an interaction that holds atoms or ions together in a stable chemical species.
The key physical question is energy: the bonded arrangement must be favourable compared with the separated pieces. Lewis ideas track valence electrons to explain many common bonding patterns.

pages.title: Draw the electrons that participate

blocks.text: A Lewis symbol places dots around an element symbol to represent valence electrons. Sodium has one dot; magnesium two; chlorine seven. Inner electrons and nucleus form the kernel and are not drawn individually.
These dots are bookkeeping symbols, not photographs of electron locations. Their number connects a main-group element’s outer configuration with its common combining capacity.

Place single valence dots around separate sides of a symbol before pairing, as a bookkeeping convention. A chlorine symbol has seven dots: three pairs and one single. The unpaired dot suggests a simple opportunity to share one pair with another atom.

pages.title: Explain electron transfer with charge balance

blocks.text: Sodium can lose one electron to form Na⁺ with a neon-like configuration; chlorine can gain one to form Cl⁻ with an argon-like configuration. Oppositely charged ions attract in the ionic solid.
For calcium fluoride, Ca²⁺ needs two F⁻ ions for neutrality, giving CaF₂. Electron transfer explains ion formation; the stabilising interactions throughout the solid complete the bonding picture.

pages.title: Share a pair instead of transferring it

blocks.text: In H₂, two H atoms share one electron pair. Each counts that pair towards a stable two-electron shell, a duplet. A shared pair represents one covalent bond, drawn as a line.
Cl₂ shares one pair while each Cl retains three lone pairs. A lone pair belongs to one atom in the Lewis representation; a bonding pair is counted around both bonded atoms.

The octet rule describes a common tendency towards eight valence electrons around an atom. Hydrogen seeks a duplet. The rule is a useful pattern, not the fundamental cause of every bond.

pages.title: Construct a Lewis structure step by step

blocks.text: For CO₂, total valence electrons=4+2×6=16. Connect O–C–O using four electrons. Complete terminal O octets, then move one lone pair from each O into bonding pairs to complete carbon’s octet.
The result O=C=O uses sixteen electrons: eight in bonds and eight in oxygen lone pairs. Each atom has an octet. Check both total electron count and each atom’s surrounding count.

pages.title: Calculate formal charge

blocks.text: Formal charge=valence electrons−non-bonding electrons−half the bonding electrons. It assigns the bonding electrons equally, making it a bookkeeping charge rather than a measured partial charge.
For NH₄⁺, N contributes five valence electrons, has zero non-bonding electrons and eight bonding electrons: FC(N)=5−0−4=+1. Each H has 1−0−1=0; the sum is+1.

blocks.text: BF₃ has only six electrons around B in its simple Lewis structure. NO has an odd total electron count, preventing all atoms from having paired octets. Expanded-octet Lewis representations occur for species such as PF₅ and SF₆.

Never invent extra electrons to force every species into an octet. The structure must retain the actual electron total and ionic charge. Second-period atoms do not expand their valence shell in this elementary treatment.

Clarification: expanded-octet drawings are useful bookkeeping. Modern bonding does not require literal occupation of low-energy valence d hybrids to explain every hypervalent main-group molecule; later textbook hybridisation labels are models, not direct measurements.

subtopics.title: Fundamentals of Thermodynamics: Systems… · Internal Energy and Adiabatic Processes

pages.title: Follow the energy, not just the flame

blocks.text: A cup of tea cools, a fuel burns and a battery powers a lamp. In each case energy passes between things. Chemistry needs a way to account for that energy even when we cannot watch individual molecules.

Thermodynamics studies energy changes in macroscopic systems: samples containing very large numbers of particles. It compares initial and final states. It tells us about energy requirements and possible directions of change, rather than how quickly a reaction happens.
Macroscopic means large enough to describe through bulk measurements such as temperature and pressure. You need not track the motion of every molecule.

pages.title: Draw an imaginary boundary

blocks.text: The system is the part of the universe selected for study. Everything outside it is the surroundings. A boundary, real or imaginary, separates the two; the system and surroundings together make the universe for the thermodynamic discussion.

To study water heated in a beaker, choose the water as the system. The beaker, hot plate and room are surroundings. Energy crossing the water boundary matters; the boundary itself is not necessarily a physical insulating wall.
A system is not automatically the entire apparatus. State your choice before deciding whether heat or matter has crossed its boundary.

pages.title: Open: both matter and energy can cross

blocks.text: Steam escaping from an uncovered vessel carries matter away. Energy can also enter from the hot plate and leave into the room. A system that can exchange both matter and energy with its surroundings is an open system.

Water in an open beaker is a useful example. Its mass may fall as it evaporates, while its temperature changes as it exchanges energy. An open system does not have to exchange both at every instant; its boundary permits both.

pages.title: Closed is different from isolated

blocks.text: A closed system exchanges energy but not matter. An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings. These are statements about the chosen boundary, not merely about whether a lid is visible.

A sealed conducting vessel can gain heat while retaining its contents, so it is closed. An ideal sealed, rigid, perfectly insulated vessel with no other work exchange is isolated. A real thermos flask approximates isolation; it is not perfectly insulated forever.
Insulation alone prevents heat transfer, not every possible energy transfer. Mechanical or electrical work may still cross an appropriately designed boundary.

pages.title: A state is described by properties

blocks.text: The state of a thermodynamic system is specified by suitable macroscopic properties, called state variables or state functions. Pressure p, volume V, temperature T and amount n help describe a gas at equilibrium.

For an ideal gas, pV = nRT links these properties, so they are not all independent. If n, T and V are fixed, p follows. Here R is the gas constant, T is in kelvin, and units must be mutually consistent.
Equilibrium here means the bulk properties are stable under the specified conditions. Measurements are compared after the system has settled.

pages.title: The route and the destination are different ideas

blocks.text: Two journeys can reach the same height by different paths. The height difference depends only on the endpoints, even though the walking distance does not. Similarly, a state-function change depends only on the initial and final states.

Internal energy U is a state function. Its change is ΔU = U(final) − U(initial). The symbol Δ means final minus initial; the SI unit of energy is the joule, J. Different procedures producing the same endpoints give the same ΔU.
This does not mean every energy transfer is path-independent. Heat and work describe transfer during a process; they are not contents stored in the system.

pages.title: Internal energy belongs to the sample

blocks.text: Internal energy includes microscopic kinetic and potential contributions within the system, including molecular motion and interactions between particles. Chemical changes can alter these contributions even when the sample looks unchanged.
We usually measure changes in U rather than assign a measurable absolute zero of internal energy. If a process raises the system energy, ΔU is positive; if it lowers it, ΔU is negative.
Stirring water can warm it without adding a hot substance. The moving paddle transfers energy through work, showing that heating is not the only way to change internal energy.

pages.title: Adiabatic means no heat transfer

blocks.text: An adiabatic process transfers no heat across the system boundary: q = 0. An adiabatic wall is an ideal insulating wall. The system can still receive or deliver work, so its internal energy and temperature can change.

In an insulated vessel, a paddle driven from outside does work on water. The water can warm even though no heat crosses the wall. Adiabatic does not mean constant temperature; constant temperature is called isothermal.
An adiabatic system is not necessarily isolated. Isolation also excludes work and matter exchange.

pages.title: An energy difference from an insulated experiment

blocks.text: For a closed system undergoing an adiabatic process, ΔU = w(ad). Work done on the system is positive; work delivered by the system is negative. Both w and ΔU are measured in J or the same energy unit.

Teacher-created example: an insulated paddle experiment transfers 150 J of work to the water. Given q = 0 and w(ad) = +150 J, the internal-energy change is ΔU = +150 J. The plus sign means the water has gained energy; it does not tell us its final temperature without further information.

questions.question: Why is water in a sealed metal vessel closed rather than isolated?
questions.answer: Matter cannot leave, but energy can cross the conducting wall. An isolated boundary would also prevent energy transfer.

questions.question: Can an adiabatic sample become warmer?
questions.answer: Yes. Work, such as stirring, can transfer energy into it even when heat transfer is zero.

questions.question: Two paths give identical initial and final states. Must ΔU be the same?
questions.answer: Yes. U is a state function, so its change depends only on those endpoints.

questions.question: An adiabatic gas delivers 80 J of work. What is ΔU?
questions.answer: Work done by the system is w = −80 J. With q = 0, ΔU = −80 J, an internal-energy decrease.

questions.question: Does a thermodynamically possible reaction necessarily occur rapidly?
questions.answer: No. Thermodynamics considers energy and direction; the rate of reaching the final state requires kinetic information.

pages.title: A bottle can look still while molecules move

blocks.text: Water in a closed bottle eventually maintains a steady liquid level. Has evaporation stopped? Molecules still leave the liquid, while others return from the vapour. An unchanging appearance can hide two continuing processes.
Dynamic equilibrium means opposing processes occur at equal rates, giving no net macroscopic change under fixed conditions. Dynamic means microscopic activity continues.

pages.title: Evaporation meets condensation

blocks.text: Initially little vapour is present, so evaporation dominates. As vapour accumulates, more molecules return to the liquid by condensation. Eventually the rates become equal.

Equilibrium vapour pressure is the pressure of vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at the specified temperature, while both phases remain. Equal rates do not mean equal amounts of liquid and vapour.
A phase is a physically uniform form such as liquid water or water vapour. Particles can move between coexisting phases.

pages.title: Boiling compares two pressures

blocks.text: Boiling occurs when liquid vapour pressure matches external pressure. Since vapour pressure rises with temperature, lower external pressure allows boiling at a lower temperature.

Water boils below 100 °C at high altitude because atmospheric pressure is lower. Its normal boiling point is approximately 100 °C at 1 atm, about 1.013 bar. Evaporation can occur below the boiling point; boiling is not the first moment any molecule escapes.

pages.title: Ice and water can coexist

blocks.text: At the melting temperature and specified pressure, molecules leave ice while others join it from liquid water. Equal melting and freezing rates preserve the relative amounts when no net heat input drives further phase change.

pages.title: Solid–vapour equilibrium

blocks.text: Sublimation is solid → vapour; deposition is vapour → solid. In a closed vessel at fixed temperature these opposing processes can balance.

pages.title: A saturated solution is still active

blocks.text: A saturated solution is in equilibrium with undissolved solute at the specified temperature. Dissolution and crystallisation continue at equal rates, so dissolved concentration stays constant.

pages.title: Why opened soda releases gas

blocks.text: In a sealed carbonated drink, CO₂ enters and leaves the liquid dynamically. Opening lowers CO₂ pressure above the liquid, so escape temporarily exceeds return and bubbles form.

pages.title: The classical definitions describe familiar reactions

blocks.text: Classically, oxidation includes addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen; reduction includes removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen. These ideas explain many familiar conversions but do not cover every redox process directly.
In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, copper oxide loses oxygen and is reduced; hydrogen gains oxygen and is oxidised. Both changes occur in the same balanced reaction. In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, magnesium gains oxygen.

pages.title: Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains them

blocks.text: Oxidation: electron loss. Reduction: electron gain. For zinc, Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. For copper ions, Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). Each equation is a half-reaction describing one side of the coupled process.
The lost and gained electron counts must agree because the overall reaction conserves electric charge.
An electron has negative charge. Losing electrons makes a species more positive; gaining electrons makes it less positive or more negative.

pages.title: Agents do the opposite to their own change

blocks.text: An oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidised. In the zinc–copper reaction, Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent and Zn is the reducing agent.

In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, sodium donates electrons and chlorine accepts them. Sodium is oxidised despite oxygen being absent. Chlorine is reduced, even though its name contains no clue about the electron transfer.

blocks.text: Copper can displace silver from an appropriate silver-ion solution: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag. Copper supplies two electrons; two silver ions accept one each. Zinc can similarly displace copper ions.

pages.title: Why does carbon appear everywhere?

blocks.text: A cotton shirt, cooking oil and a medicine look unrelated, yet their compounds contain carbon. Organic chemistry gives us a common way to understand such substances through their bonding and structures, rather than memorising every material separately.

Some simple carbon compounds, such as carbon oxides and carbonates, are conventionally studied in inorganic chemistry.

pages.title: Carbon chains need a structural language

blocks.text: A molecular formula gives atom numbers but not their connections. C2H6O, for example, does not tell us whether oxygen connects to hydrogen or lies between two carbon groups. Structural formulas show connectivity, which is essential for explaining properties and reactions.

pages.title: Shape comes from the bonds

blocks.text: Carbon does not always have the same geometry. Hybridisation describes combinations of atomic orbitals used to explain bonding directions. In methane, four sp3 orbitals point towards the corners of a tetrahedron; the H–C–H angle is about 109.5°, rather than the 90° suggested by a flat cross.

Each carbon in ethene is sp2 hybridised: three bond directions lie in a plane at about 120°. Each carbon in ethyne is sp hybridised: its two bond directions lie along a straight line, giving 180°. These shapes describe the region around that carbon, not every atom in a larger molecule.

pages.title: Sigma and pi bonds do different jobs

blocks.text: A sigma (σ) bond forms by head-on orbital overlap along the line joining two nuclei. A pi (π) bond forms by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below that line. A single bond is σ; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π.

Count bonds in ethene, CH2=CH2. Four C–H bonds contribute four σ bonds. The C=C bond contributes one σ and one π bond. Total: five σ and one π. Counting the double bond as two σ bonds would give the wrong picture of its geometry and reactivity.

pages.title: Why a double bond resists rotation

blocks.text: The two p orbitals forming a π bond must remain parallel. Twisting one carbon relative to the other reduces their sideways overlap. Free rotation about C=C would therefore disrupt the π bond and requires much more energy than ordinary rotation about a C–C single bond.

The exposed π electron cloud also helps explain why multiple bonds are sites of chemical attack. Notice the link: the same orbital arrangement influences both molecular shape and reactivity. This does not mean that every reaction of a double bond happens under the same conditions.

questions.question: How many σ and π bonds are present in HC≡CH?

pages.title: From cooking fuel to carbon skeletons

blocks.text: LPG in a kitchen and petrol in a vehicle are familiar uses of hydrocarbons. These fuels contain compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen. Their structures also make hydrocarbons useful starting materials for polymers and many other chemicals, so the chapter is about more than burning fuels.

A hydrocarbon contains only C and H. Carbon–carbon bond types separate saturated compounds, containing only single bonds, from unsaturated compounds with multiple bonds. Aromatic hydrocarbons form a special class of cyclic structures with characteristic stability and reactions.

blocks.text: Open-chain saturated hydrocarbons are alkanes; saturated carbon rings are cycloalkanes. Alkenes contain C=C and alkynes C≡C. Benzene is aromatic rather than an ordinary alkene, despite being drawn with multiple bonds in familiar structural representations.
